# Principles

These are the principles of the strategy program. The same fourteen apply across the program's
courses and clubs, here applied to running a club.

Each principle carries a scripture reference, collected at the [end of this
page](#scripture-references).

The sources they draw on, following Brigham Young's admonition to gather up all
the good and true principles wherever we find them: the [BYU Marriott mission and
values](https://marriott.byu.edu/our-story/mission/), the standard works, [Christlike
Attributes](https://www.churchofjesuschrist.org/study/manual/preach-my-gospel-2023/14-chapter-6?lang=eng)
from Preach My Gospel, [Amazon's leadership
principles](https://www.amazon.jobs/content/en/our-workplace/leadership-principles),
[Bridgewater's original philosophy](https://www.bridgewater.com/culture/bridgewaters-original-philosophy),
[McKinsey's purpose, mission and values](https://www.mckinsey.com/about-us/overview/our-purpose-mission-and-values),
[John Wooden's Pyramid of Success](https://coachwooden.com/pyramid-of-success), and
[Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics, Book II](https://classics.mit.edu/Aristotle/nicomachaen.2.ii.html).

## Why They Are Written This Way

Most codes of conduct list principles to be maximized: be excellent, be truthful, be bold.
Stated that way they have two problems.

The first is that almost any good quality can be taken to excess. Truthfulness can overshoot
into cruelty. Excellence can overshoot into perfectionism, or into standards that humiliate
people. Initiative can overshoot into recklessness. A list of maxims gives you no way to say
"you are doing too much of a good thing," so the only correction on offer is to abandon the
principle, which nobody wants.

The second is that two good principles collide. Speed collides with rigor. Candor collides
with charity. Excellence collides with a deadline.

Aristotle solved both with the **golden mean**. Every good quality of character sits between
two failure modes, one of doing too little and one of doing too much. Courage is not the
opposite of cowardice; it sits between cowardice and recklessness. Generosity sits between
stinginess and waste. The failure is never the quality itself. It is having too little or too
much of it, at the wrong moment, toward the wrong person, for the wrong reason.

The mean is not fixed by a formula. It is found by judgment, and judgment is built by
practice. Each principle below is written with both of its failures named, because you cannot
aim for the mean if you do not know the extremes.

These are aspirational. Everyone misses, often, in both directions. We keep striving, and
over time develop true wisdom.

> Success is peace of mind which is a direct result of self-satisfaction in knowing you made
> the effort to become the best of which you are capable.
>
> John Wooden

## 1. Hold to the truth, and use it well

| Principle | Too little | The golden mean | Too much |
|---|---|---|---|
| Act with integrity | Deceitful | States it plainly, including the part that costs something | Self-righteous |
| Be discerning | Repeats what was said in confidence. Says the true thing that only wounds | Tells the person who needs it, in the way they can receive it | Calls it discretion when it is avoidance |
| Be courageous | Goes along | Challenges, then commits | Fights for ego |

## 2. Think hard and stay teachable

| Principle | Too little | The golden mean | Too much |
|---|---|---|---|
| Be curious | Accepts the brief as given. Stops at the first answer | Asks the question behind the question | Chases the interesting question instead of the one that matters |
| Be rigorous | Accepts what sounds right. Trusts the output without checking the reasoning | Reasons from first principles | Rederives what is already settled. Demands proof past the point the decision needs |
| Choose humility | Defends the position instead of testing it. Ties ego to being right | Asks what they missed, then changes | Hedges. Defers when they know better |
| Seek personal improvement | Hears the feedback and files it | Asks for the critique, then acts on it | Works on themselves instead of the work. Makes every review about their growth |

## 3. Do great work

| Principle | Too little | The golden mean | Too much |
|---|---|---|---|
| Act in faith | Waits for certainty. Needs the risk gone before starting | Moves on incomplete information | Skips the preparation and calls it faith |
| Strive for excellence | Settles for what passes. Mistakes activity for achievement | Raises the bar, then clears it | Polishes past the point of value. Wields the standard to shame |
| Demonstrate high agency | Waits to be told. Explains why it was not theirs | Sees the gap and closes it | Takes what was not theirs to take. Carries it alone instead of raising it |
| Show patience | Forces the answer before it is ready. Quits when it gets hard | Presses where it can move, waits where it cannot | Waits and calls it patience. Tolerates what should have been escalated |

## 4. Make each other better

| Principle | Too little | The golden mean | Too much |
|---|---|---|---|
| Respect others | Talks past people. Dismisses the junior voice | Listens before answering | Trades candor for comfort. Plays favorites |
| Forgive quickly | Keeps score. Lets it color the next interaction | Says it once, then lets it go | Forgives before anything is named, so the pattern repeats |
| Develop others | Keeps what they know. Treats a teammate as a pair of hands | Hands it over and explains the why | Does it for them instead of with them |

## For Some Things There Is No Golden Mean

Almost everything above is a matter of degree. A few things are not. Aristotle is explicit
that the doctrine has limits: some acts "imply by their names that they are themselves bad,"
and of those "it is not possible, then, ever to be right with regard to them." There is no
correct amount of them, so they are not on the scale.

## When Principles Collide

They will. Rigor says check it again; the deadline says ship. Courage says say it now;
discernment says not in this room, not in front of these people. Excellence says raise the
bar; patience says this is not the week.

There is no rule that decides. Aristotle says the judgment "rests with perception," meaning
the read of a person who is actually present and has done this before. That is why the answer
to a hard call is usually a conversation rather than a lookup.

Three practical aids.

**Name the collision out loud.** "I think rigor and the deadline are fighting here" is a
faster route to a decision than arguing the merits as though only one principle were in play.

**Correct against your own pull.** Aiming straight at the mean undershoots, because your own
habit is already bending you. Learn which way you personally miss, then overcorrect. "We
shall get into the intermediate state by drawing well away from error, as people do in
straightening sticks that are bent."

**The red face test.** When a situation is genuinely ambiguous, ask whether you could explain
the decision to a respected leader without being red in the face. If not, do not do it.

## Which Way Did I Miss?

The most useful question you can ask a peer, given how this page is written, is directional:
**which way did I miss, too little or too much?**

That is far easier for a teammate to answer than a rating, and it is the only kind of answer
you can act on. Use it in your [feedback conversations](04-peer-feedback.qmd), and use it
after any meeting or event you ran.

## Scripture References

Each entry names the commitment or principle it belongs to, so this section can be read on
its own. These are not proof texts. They are the older statement of the same idea, and in
several cases they name both failures at once, which is the whole reason this page is written
the way it is.

and as they are to come.

**Act with integrity**

*Doctrine and Covenants 124:15* And again, verily I say unto you, blessed is my servant Hyrum

**Be discerning**

*Proverbs 25:11* A word fitly spoken is like apples of gold in pictures of silver.

**Be courageous**

*Doctrine and Covenants 121:43* Reproving betimes with sharpness, when moved upon by the Holy

*Joshua 1:9* Have not I commanded thee? Be strong and of a good courage; be not afraid,
